FINSAFETYBENCH: Evaluating LLM Safety in Real-World Financial
Scenarios
Yutao Hou1*, Yihan Jiang1* , Yuhan Xie1, Jian Yang2, Liwen Zhang1
Hailiang Huang1†, Guanhua Chen3† , Yun Chen1,4†
1Shanghai University of Finance and Economics, 2Beihang University
3Southern University of Science and Technology
4MoE Key Laboratory of Interdisciplinary Research of Computation and Economics
Abstract
Large language models (LLMs) are increas-
ingly applied in financial scenarios. However,
they may produce harmful outputs, including
facilitating illegal activities or unethical be-
havior, posing serious compliance risks. To
systematically evaluate LLM safety in finance,
we propose FINSAFETYBENCH, a bilingual
(English-Chinese) red-teaming benchmark de-
signed to test an LLM’s refusal of requests
that violate financial compliance. Grounded
in real-world financial crime cases and ethics
standards, the benchmark comprises 14 subcat-
egories spanning financial crimes and ethical
violations. Through extensive experiments on
general-purpose and finance-specialized LLMs
under three representative attack settings, we
identify critical vulnerabilities that allow adver-
sarial prompts to bypass compliance safeguards.
Further analysis reveals stronger susceptibility
in Chinese contexts and highlights the limita-
tions of prompt-level defenses against sophisti-
cated or implicit manipulation strategies.
Warning: This paper contains prompts from
illegal or unethical financial scenarios that
may be offensive.
1
Introduction
Recent large language models (LLMs) have shown
strong capabilities in understanding and generating
financial text (Nie et al., 2024b; Ding et al., 2024;
Zhao et al., 2024; Zhang and Yang, 2023). These
capabilities make LLMs promising tools for a wide
range of financial applications, including invest-
ment decision-making (Yang et al., 2023; Li et al.,
2025; Kundu et al., 2025), financial reasoning (Zhu
et al., 2025b; Srivastava et al., 2024; Khatuya et al.,
2025), and market analysis (Chen et al., 2024b;
Wang et al., 2024). While these advances create
significant opportunities, regulators and policymak-
ers have raised concerns about potential misuse.

In particular, LLMs could be exploited to conceal
accounting fraud, manipulate financial reports, or
fabricate transactions, which poses risks to mar-
ket integrity and financial stability. This misuse,
compounded by the models’ inherent susceptibil-
ity to misinformation and adversarial manipula-
tion (Yang et al., 2025a), not only violates legal and
ethical standards but also damages investor trust.
Therefore, systematically evaluating the safety of
LLMs in finance is an urgent research priority.
Existing financial benchmarks mainly target
knowledge-based question answering (Chen et al.,
2024a; Lu et al., 2023; Zhu et al., 2024) and com-
plex reasoning (Xie et al., 2024a; Lu et al., 2025;
Chen et al., 2021; Yoash et al., 2025; Xie et al.,
2025; Jiang et al., 2025), thereby facilitating the
evaluation of market prediction, numerical rea-
soning, and financial decision-making. However,
these benchmarks overlook the potential misuse
of LLMs for illicit or unethical financial activities.
Although general safety and compliance bench-
marks exist (Zhang et al., 2023; Xu et al., 2024;
Nie et al., 2024a; Zhang et al., 2024; Chao et al.,
2024; Mazeika et al., 2024; Hui et al., 2025; Bhard-
waj and Poria, 2023; Qi et al., 2024), they predom-
inantly focus on coarse-grained ethical categories
and contain limited finance-specific scenarios. Fur-
thermore, the reliance on LLM-synthesized data
in some studies (Hui et al., 2025; Bhardwaj and
Poria, 2023) introduces redundancy and constrains
data validity to the generator’s domain competence.
These limitations hinder the identification of fine-
grained compliance risks and impede rigorous eval-
uation of LLM safety in financial settings.
To mitigate this gap, we introduce FINSAFE-
TYBENCH, a bilingual (English–Chinese) finan-
cial red-teaming benchmark derived from real-
world cases.
Compared with existing financial
red-teaming benchmarks, FINSAFETYBENCH pro-
vides several advantages: (1) Real-world applica-
bility. Existing financial benchmarks mainly evalu-

FINSAFETYBENCH instead focuses on concrete
violation scenarios, better reflecting real-world
cases of LLM misuse in finance. (2) Diversity
and information richness. FINSAFETYBENCH is
sourced from real-world cases rather than model-
generated data, reducing duplication and model
dependence. Each entry documents authentic vi-
olations and provides richer context for evaluat-
ing models in realistic and complex scenarios. (3)
Fine-grained and systematic categorization. Unlike
the coarse-grained categorizations of prior bench-
marks (Zhang et al., 2023; Xu et al., 2024), FIN-
SAFETYBENCH introduces a systematic taxonomy
consisting of two major categories and fourteen
subcategories. (4) Multilingual support. Including
Chinese and English data enables a more compre-
hensive cross-lingual assessment of LLM safety in
finance.
With FINSAFETYBENCH, we evaluate main-
stream open-source models against three represen-
tative jailbreak attacks. We find that some attack
variants achieve notably high success rates, and
the models demonstrate greater vulnerability when
evaluated on Chinese data. Further experiments re-
veal that common prompt-level defenses have cer-
tain limitations against complex or implicit adver-
sarial strategies, which underscores the inadequacy
of current LLMs in financial safety scenarios.
Our contributions are summarized as follows:
• We propose FINSAFETYBENCH, a bilingual red-
teaming benchmark grounded in real-world cases
to facilitate rigorous safety evaluation in the fi-
nancial domain.
• We define a fine-grained taxonomy of financial
misuse, covering 11 types of financial crimes and
3 categories of ethical violations, filling the gap
in finance-specific safety alignment.
• Through comprehensive jailbreak and defense
experiments, we show that LLMs are vulnerable
in financial scenarios and that existing prompt-
engineering defenses have certain limitations
against sophisticated attacks.1
2
Related Work
2.1
Financial Benchmark
Existing financial benchmarks predominantly as-
sess knowledge-based question answering (Shah
et al., 2022; Lu et al., 2023; Zhu et al., 2024; Yang
et al., 2024) and reasoning (Chen et al., 2021,
2022; Yoash et al., 2025), and evolving toward
higher complexity (Chen et al., 2024a; Xie et al.,
2024a; Hou et al., 2024), broader coverage (Jiang
et al., 2025; Li et al., 2025), and comprehensive
metrics (Lu et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2025; Xie
et al., 2025). However, financial safety remains
significantly underexplored compared to capability
evaluations. For example, FinEval (Zhang et al.,
2023) prioritizes domain knowledge over misuse
risks, while SuperCLUE-Fin (Xu et al., 2024) and
CFinBench (Nie et al., 2024a) target regulatory
backgrounds rather than practical attacks. Simi-
larly, OpenFinData (East et al., 2023) and the Cu-
pace Financial LLM Evaluation Dataset (Shanghai
AI Lab. et al., 2024) address compliance but suf-
fer from limited transparency due to closed-source
data (summarized in Table 1). To address this gap,
we introduce FINSAFETYBENCH, a specialized
benchmark designed to evaluate financial safety
and reveal robustness vulnerabilities under diverse
jailbreak scenarios.
2.2
LLM Safety

prompt engineering into automated paradigms, in-
cluding gradient-optimized adversarial suffix in-

algorithm-guided generation (Liu et al., 2023b),
tree-of-thought refinement (Mehrotra et al., 2024),
character-level manipulations (Yang et al., 2025b),
and dynamic prompt iteration (Liu et al., 2024b;

Such vul-
nerabilities are especially critical when deploying
parameter-efficient fine-tuning (Hu et al., 2021;
Wang et al., 2025) for domain adaptation. In re-
sponse, comprehensive safety evaluation frame-
works have emerged, supported by general-purpose
benchmarks. For example, JailbreakBench (Chao
et al., 2024) evaluates the robustness of LLMs
against jailbreak attacks, and SORRY-Bench (Xie
et al., 2024b) evaluates safety, including linguistic
and prompt-formatting factors. Similarly, Chinese-
context benchmarks such as FLAMES (Huang
et al., 2024), SuperCLUE-Safety (Xu et al., 2023),
and jailBench (Liu et al., 2025) target com-
prehensive safety assessments.
However, fine-
grained evaluations tailored to the highly regulated,
security-critical financial domain are still scarce.
Recently, TRIDENT (Hui et al., 2025) introduced
a financial safety benchmark grounded in the CFA
Institute Code of Ethics. Although principled, its
heavy dependence on specific Code provisions lim-
its case diversity and fails to capture real-world
variations. In contrast, FINSAFETYBENCH derives
from documented real-world cases; each entry con-
stitutes a complete scenario, resulting in broader
coverage and more realistic simulations.
3
FINSAFETYBENCH Construction
3.1
Overview
An overview of FINSAFETYBENCH is shown in
Figure 1. We collect real-world financial miscon-
duct cases, including legal judgments and CFA
ethics materials, filtered and rephrased by LLMs
into harmful instructions. The dataset comprises
1,201 proprietary cases and 680 samples from
external sources (TRIDENT (Hui et al., 2025),
HarmfulQA (Bhardwaj and Poria, 2023), and HEx-
PHI (Qi et al., 2024)), yielding 1,881 bilingually
aligned instances. Below, we present a breakdown
of the categories and data construction pipeline.
3.2
Problem Categories
To enable comprehensive evaluation, we define a
two-level taxonomy comprising severe financial
crimes and financial ethical violations that remain
essential for safety despite their lower severity. Fig-
ure 2 illustrates the hierarchical structure of these
categories. The detailed definitions of all categories
are provided in Appendix C.
Financial Crimes
This category encompasses
illegal activities within the financial industry that
inflict serious societal harm, often cause major fi-
nancial losses, and may result in criminal prose-
cution. These activities constitute critical threats
that LLM safety alignment must address. Drawing
on relevant provisions of Chinese Criminal Law,
our benchmark covers 11 representative types of
financial crimes: Market Manipulation, Bribery,
Insider Trading, Misappropriation of funds, Fraud,

resentation, False Invoicing, and Cybercrime.
Financial ethical violations
This category cov-
ers behaviors of financial practitioners that violate
widely accepted ethical standards or company reg-
ulations during their professional activities. Al-
though their direct harm is generally less severe
than that of financial crimes, they can still under-
mine client or employer interests as well as mar-
ket integrity, and thus demand significant attention.
Referencing the CFA Institute’s Code of Ethics2,
we identified the following three types of miscon-
duct: Harming Customer Interests, Harming Em-
ployer Interests, and Lack of Independence and
Objectivity.
3.3
Data Construction
3.3.1
Data sources and selection criteria
We collect raw material from three complementary
streams:
Financial judicial and legal case materials
We
manually collect publicly available judicial judg-
ments and legal documents related to financial
crimes3, which provide detailed descriptions of
offender behavior. These sources capture realis-
tic operational patterns and legally verified facts
across multiple categories of financial crime. All

data are publicly accessible and may be used for
academic research purposes.
Publicly accessible mock exams
We gather pub-
licly available CFA mock exam questions, each
containing a fictional but realistic scenario. These
questions are then consolidated and adapted to pre-
vent copyright issues while maintaining their edu-
cational and research value.
Public released red-teaming datasets
We ex-
tract financial examples from TRIDENT (Hui et al.,
2025), HarmfulQA (Bhardwaj and Poria, 2023),
and HExPHI (Qi et al., 2024). From these corpora,
we filter only instances of LLM refusals satisfying
our pipeline criteria.
3.3.2
Data Processing
Inspired by recent studies on LLM’s ability to as-
sist human annotation (Zhang et al., 2024; Liang
et al., 2025; Tang et al., 2025; Zhu et al., 2025a), we
design a pipeline to transform real-world financial
cases into financial violation scenarios. The data
processing pipeline comprises five stages: (1) ex-
traction and summarization, (2) controlled rephras-
ing and harmfulness verification, (3) selection and
integration of public datasets, (4) bilingual align-
ment, and (5) deduplication and dataset assembly.
We design these stages to preserve realism while in-
corporating financial harm, thereby eliciting LLM
refusal behavior.
Extraction and summarization
In this stage, we
first extract textual content from the collected doc-
uments (PDF format) by open-source extraction
tools4. Given the length and level of irrelevant
detail in judicial precedents, we employ Qwen3-
32B to extract criminal behavioral patterns and the
implicated legal provisions. (see Appendix B.1 for
details). In contrast, for CFA cases with high in-
formation density, we combine the entire problem
and its corresponding answer into a single seed
instance. Since CFA items lack explicit categoriza-
tion, we design a targeted classification prompt (see
Appendix B.2) and use Qwen3-32B to categorize
and label them. After manual verification of each
item, all processed texts are used as seed data for
the subsequent stage.
Controlled rephrasing and harmfulness veri-
fication
We employ Deepseek-V3 (Liu et al.,
2024a) with carefully designed prompts (see Ap-
pendix B.3) to convert seeds into instruction-style
4https://github.com/datalab-to/marker

Chinese user queries. We select Deepseek-V3 for
its state-of-the-art performance in Chinese tasks
and strong reasoning capabilities. For harmful-
ness verification, we generate reference responses
using Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct (Qwen et al., 2025),
which serves as a representative target model due
to its robust instruction-following capabilities. We
validate the harmfulness of the rephrased queries
based on these outputs; specifically, we retain only
those queries that consistently elicit explicit and
non-actionable refusals from the model.
Selection and integration of public datasets
We
filter publicly available datasets (TRIDENT (Hui
et al., 2025), HarmfulQA (Bhardwaj and Poria,
2023), and HExPHI (Qi et al., 2024)) and incor-
porate the financial instances into FINSAFETY-
BENCH. To ensure consistency, we apply the afore-
mentioned harmfulness verification and categoriza-
tion to these external samples before integration.
Bilingual alignment
We employ a controlled
translation pipeline to produce bilingual versions
(Chinese and English) for each item. Qwen3-32B
generates the initial translations, which human an-
notators subsequently verify to ensure semantic
equivalence between the two languages.
Deduplication and dataset assembly
Following
FinGPT (Liu et al., 2023a), we apply a MinHash-
based LSH approach to identify near-duplicate
texts and retain only the most representative in-
stance among highly similar samples. The resulting
collection constitutes the final benchmark, where
each data entry comprises the harmful instruction,
category, language label, and source tag.
3.3.3
Quality Control
To ensure the reliability of FINSAFETYBENCH, we
invite graduate students in finance to execute a rig-
orous multi-stage verification protocol, as detailed
in Appendix M. First, regarding source integrity,
they validate each real-world judicial case and CFA
mock exam question to guarantee accuracy. Sub-
sequently, they manually review the intermediate
summarizations generated by Qwen3-32B to miti-
gate potential hallucinations or biases introduced
by the LLM. Finally, for the red-team instructions
rephrased by DeepSeek-V3 and items integrated
from public datasets, these students conduct a thor-
ough validation to ensure that both Chinese and
English versions are consistently harmful and cor-
rectly categorized.
4
Experiments
4.1
Experiment Setup
Evaluation Models
We evaluate six target
models on FINSAFETYBENCH, comprising five
general-domain LLMs and one finance-specific
model.
The general models are LLaMA-
3 (AI@Meta, 2024) (Meta-Llama-3-8B-Instruct),
InternLM3 (Cai et al., 2024) (InternLM3-8B-
Instruct), GLM-4 (GLM et al., 2024) (GLM-4-9B-
0414), Mistral (Mistral AI Team, 2025) (Mistral-
Small-24B-Instruct-2501), and Qwen2.5 (Qwen
et al., 2025) (Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct), and one
finance-specific model: XuanYuan (Zhang and
Yang, 2023) (XuanYuan-13B-Chat). These models
range in size from 8B to 32B and cover general
and finance-specialized variants. This allows us
to analyze how model scale and domain expertise
affect robustness against jailbreak attacks in the
financial domain. We additionally evaluate their
baseline performance under original non-jailbroken
prompts, finding that general-purpose models main-
tain near-zero baseline ASRs, while XuanYuan ex-
hibits higher inherent vulnerability (detailed in Ap-
pendix G).
Implementation Details of Jailbreak and De-
fense
We conduct jailbreak experiments us-

Detailed de-

Specifically, we employ three attack methods:
PAIR (n_streams=5, n_iterations=3, attack
model: Qwen3-32B), ReNeLLM (iter_max=3,
attack model:
Qwen3-32B), and FlipAttack
(flip_mode=FCS, cot=lang_gpt).
For defense,
we evaluate three prompt-based strategies: Self-
Reminder (Xie et al., 2023), In-Context Defense
(ICD) (Wei et al., 2023), and Fin-Guard. While
the first two are general-purpose techniques, Fin-
Guard is a domain-specific defense we designed
that explicitly incorporates financial safety con-
straints into the model’s system instructions.

Chao et al., 2024), we use the Attack Success Rate
(ASR) as our primary metric, employing Qwen3-
32B as the evaluator. The scoring scale ranges
from 1 to 10, where 1 indicates a full refusal, and
10 denotes a complete violation with a comprehen-
sive answer to the malicious request. The specific

4.2
Main Results
Table 2 presents the average ASR across three at-
tack methods for six LLMs, while Figure 3 details
performance across 14 subcategories. Comprehen-
sive results are provided in Appendix F.
Model-wise results
We observe substantial vari-
ance in robustness, indicating that vulnerability
is not solely dependent on model scale.
Mis-
tral proves the most vulnerable with average
ASRs exceeding 90% in both languages, followed
closely by Qwen2.5. Conversely, LLaMA-3 and
XuanYuan yield significantly lower ASRs, with
LLaMA-3 recording the lowest overall figure,
likely stemming from the rigorous safety alignment
integrated throughout its training stages (AI@Meta,
2024). Similarly, XuanYuan exhibits superior ro-
bustness compared to general-purpose models, im-
plying potential benefits from its financial-domain
tuning.
These findings suggest that robustness
stems primarily from explicit safety alignment and
domain grounding rather than model scale. To val-
idate this, we conducted a controlled intra-family
comparison between Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct and
its 72B variant (Appendix H). The 72B model
shows no safety improvement and is even slightly
more vulnerable, confirming that scaling parame-
ters alone do not mitigate financial safety risks.
Attack-wise effectiveness
Our analysis high-
lights distinct performance patterns across different
attack methods. Iterative approaches, such as PAIR
and ReNeLLM, achieve high ASRs. They progres-
sively refine inputs to bypass safeguards, maintain-
ing high effectiveness despite their computational
costs. Conversely, FlipAttack shows extreme insta-
bility. Its ASR reaches 93.3% against Mistral but
drops sharply to 6.5% against XuanYuan. This dis-
crepancy likely stems from XuanYuan’s tendency
to prioritize the explicit character-flipping instruc-
tion, effectively overlooking the underlying mali-
cious intent. Overall, these results indicate that
iterative refinement strategies offer the most robust
and consistent jailbreaking capabilities.
Category-wise results
Figure 3 presents the
ASR aggregated across all models, revealing a sig-
nificant vulnerability gap where Financial Crimes
consistently yield higher ASRs compared to Ethical
Violations. In particular, False Invoicing and
Misappropriation of Funds emerge as the most
susceptible subcategories. We attribute this dis-
parity to the operational nature of financial crimes.

Unlike abstract ethical violations, financial miscon-
duct involves procedural steps widely documented
in judicial cases and regulatory reports. This exten-
sive exposure during training enhances the models’
instruction-following capabilities for such tasks, in-
advertently strengthening their ability to execute
crime-related instructions.
Language-wise results
As illustrated in Fig-

lingual variation. Despite the semantic equivalence

distinct susceptibility patterns: GLM-4, XuanYuan,

and InternLM3 are more vulnerable to English
prompts. These disparities suggest that current
safety mechanisms exhibit inconsistent alignment
across languages. This inconsistency likely arises
from imbalanced training data distributions or in-
trinsic language-specific biases within the models.
Consequently, our findings underscore the essential
need for comprehensive multilingual evaluations to
assess LLM safety.

5.4
Comparative Study of Three Jailbreak
Strategies
In this section, we use the Market Manipulation
category as a representative case study to exam-
ine how three distinct jailbreak strategies circum-
vent safety measures, as illustrated in Appendix Ta-
ble 18. PAIR and ReNeLLM generate diverse but
semantically equivalent variants through semantic
rewriting and word order or style changes, which
can undermine detection systems that rely solely on
surface patterns or static rules. FlipAttack applies
reversible character-level transformations and lever-
ages the model’s instruction-following behavior to
obfuscate the original intent, effectively masking
it as superficial noise. This effectively bypasses
defenses based on string matching or keywords.
5.5
Case Studies of Failure Modes in
Financial Safety
To further examine the security vulnerabilities of
LLMs in financial-safety tasks, we analyze the
mechanisms by which jailbreak techniques ma-
nipulate malicious financial inputs to elicit model
responses that should otherwise be refused. We
identify several recurrent manipulation strategies,
including role reframing, descriptive substitution

of explicitly illegal terms, endorsement by authori-
tative institutions or experts, induced urgency, fic-
tional scenarios, and strategy fusion. These strate-
gies exploit domain-specific financial terminology
and procedural workflows to bypass built-in safe-
guards. These techniques reveal systematic weak-
nesses in existing safety mechanisms when LLMs
are deployed in realistic financial settings. Detailed
definitions and representative examples of these
failure patterns are presented in Appendix P.
6
Conclusion
In this work, we introduce FINSAFETYBENCH,
a bilingual red-teaming benchmark for evaluating
LLM refusal of financial compliance violations.
The benchmark is developed based on real-world
financial crime cases and established ethical viola-
tion scenarios, encompassing 14 fine-grained cate-
gories of financial misconduct. We evaluate both
general-purpose and finance-specialized LLMs un-
der three representative jailbreak attacks and un-
cover critical vulnerabilities. We find that specific
attack variants remain consistently effective, with
models exhibiting higher susceptibility in Chinese
than in English. Furthermore, common prompt-
level defenses often fail against complex or im-
plicit adversarial strategies. These findings under-
score the urgent need for multilingual, fine-grained
safety evaluations and more robust, adaptive de-
fense mechanisms.
Limitations
While FINSAFETYBENCH emphasizes realism
through documented financial crime cases and pro-
fessional ethics standards, it nevertheless exhibits
several limitations that stem from constraints in
computational resources and human labor. First,
the dataset currently covers only English and Chi-
nese, omitting other languages. Second, model-
assisted steps for rephrasing and bilingual align-
ment, although manually validated, may still in-
troduce subtle generation biases. Third, our ex-
periments focus on a selected set of LLMs and
jailbreak strategies, potentially overlooking emerg-
ing attack techniques or defense paradigms. Future
work aims to expand language coverage, incorpo-
rate additional modalities, and investigate broader
defense strategies to enhance robustness and gener-
alizability.
Ethical Consideration
This work introduces FINSAFETYBENCH, a bilin-
gual benchmark for evaluating LLM safety and
compliance in financial scenarios. However, our
dataset contains harmful instructions, which may
pose potential risks of misuse. To mitigate this risk,
we only make the instruction portion of the dataset
publicly available and strictly limit its use to re-
search purposes, while ensuring that any harmful
outputs generated by models are fully safeguarded
from disclosure.
In constructing the dataset, we recruit three mas-
ter’s students as academic volunteers for annota-
tion. The annotators are informed in advance that
the data may contain harmful content and are al-
lowed to withdraw voluntarily at any time. Both
the recruitment process and the data collection pro-
tocol follow the institution’s current standards and
are approved by the ethics review board.

The details of jailbreak and defense
We detail three representative black-box jailbreak
techniques employed in our study.
• Prompt
Automatic
Iterative
Refinement
(PAIR): PAIR is an automated, prompt-level jail-
break method for black-box LLMs that places
an attacker model and a target model in an ad-
versarial loop. The attacker model generates a
batch of candidate jailbreak requests from an
initial prompt. Then, using fewer than twenty
black-box queries, it combines security-violation
signals from the target model’s responses with
chain-of-thought scoring to rank, filter, and se-
mantically rewrite the prompts. This iterative
process continues until it produces a highly ef-
fective prompt capable of bypassing the target
model’s safety policy.
• ReNeLLM: ReNeLLM is a fully automated jail-
break framework based on a two-stage paradigm
of prompt rewriting and scenario nesting, re-
quiring no white-box gradients or external op-
timization. It first leverages the LLM itself to
perform semantically-equivalent yet morpholog-
ically perturbed transformations on the origi-
nal harmful prompt—such as paraphrasing, mis-
spelling, code-mixing, and injecting noise—and
then randomly nests the rewritten prompt into
three generic task templates: code completion,
table filling, or text continuation. By exploiting
the model’s prioritization of task instructions, the
true intent is effectively concealed. The entire
process is scored in real time by a harmfulness
evaluator and iterates for at most 20 rounds, yield-
ing stealthy jailbreak prompts with high success
rates and cross-model transferability within min-
utes.
• FlipAttack: FlipAttack is a single-query black-
box jailbreak method that leverages the left-to-
right reading bias of autoregressive LLMs. It re-
quires no external knowledge; it simply flips the
characters or word order of the harmful prompt it-
self to generate left-side noise, thereby confusing
the target model. Then, using chain-of-thought or
role-playing prompts, it guides the model to “flip
back” and execute the hidden instruction, thus
breaching the safety guardrails with an extremely
high success rate in a single interaction.
We evaluate three prompt-based defense mecha-
nisms. The detailed prompts for each strategy are
illustrated in Figure 9.
• Self-Reminder: This method encapsulates the
user query within a system prompt to enforce
a responsible AI context, thereby explicitly dis-
couraging harmful or misleading outputs.
• In-Context Defense (ICD): A few-shot strategy
that provides a demonstration of a safe refusal
to a harmful query, guiding the model to reject
similar malicious requests.
• Fin-Guard: A domain-specific defense imple-
mented via a customized system prompt. To
bridge the gap in general alignment for finan-
cial crimes, we explicitly inject the definitions of
the 14 financial risk categories into this prompt.

LLM-Based Evaluation and Human
Evaluation Consistency Analysis
To validate Qwen3-32B as an automated judge, we
perform stratified random sampling across jailbreak
methods. For each method we sample 100 exam-
ples balanced by the automated judge’s labeled
outcome (roughly 50 judge-labeled successes and
50 judge-labeled failures). Three annotators with
graduate-level finance training independently label
each example. Annotators answer two yes/no ques-
tions per sample: (1) is the modified query harmful
(i.e., requests actionable wrongdoing)? and (2)
does the target model’s reply provide harmful/ac-
tionable assistance? A sample is considered a true
jailbreak success only if both answers are “yes.” Fi-
nal human labels are determined by majority vote.
Treating the automated judge as a binary classi-
fier (“success” vs. “failure”), the agreement sum-
mary against human consensus is: accuracy ≈
93.6%, true positive rate ≈91.5%, and false pos-
itive rate ≈4.2%. These figures indicate high
agreement between Qwen3-32B and human con-
sensus. Notably, the judge shows a conservative
bias (higher precision than recall), implying the au-
tomated ASR may slightly underestimate the true
human ASR. Overall, the validation supports us-
ing Qwen3-32B as a practical, scalable judge for
large-scale evaluation.

Case Studies of Failure Modes in
Financial Safety
Table 19 illustrates the strategies employed by cur-
rent jailbreak techniques to successfully induce
LLMs to generate harmful outputs, providing con-
crete examples of typical failure cases. The follow-

ing list presents detailed definitions and explana-
tions of each strategy.
• Role Reframing: Altering the perceived role of
the actor can cause the model to overlook the true
malicious intent, resulting in harmful responses.
For instance, when the original question involves
a “scammer”, the model can correctly recognize
the malicious intent and refuse to respond. How-
ever, reframing the actor from “a scammer de-
signing a money-laundering channel” to “a fi-
nancial engineering researcher writing a paper”
shifts the model’s focus to academic writing and
can lead it to produce content containing harmful
instructions.
• Descriptive Substitution of Explicitly Illegal
Terms: Replacing overtly illegal terminology
with a descriptive account of the same concept
can mislead the model, indicating the model’s
insufficient understanding of illicit behavior. For
example, a direct query about “insider trading”
triggers the model’s refusal, whereas phrasing
the question as “trading strategies during the sen-
sitive period of significant business integrations
not yet reflected in financial statements” can re-
sult in the model generating detailed insider trad-
ing plans.
• Endorsement by Authoritative Institutions or
Renowned Experts: Citing reputable organi-
zations or field-recognized scholars can cause
the model to misclassify content as legitimate,
facilitating jailbreaks. For instance, a direct ques-
tion regarding “transferring bribery funds” ac-
tivates safety mechanisms, but framing it as “a
case study based on IMF money-laundering re-
ports” enables the model to propose an opera-
tional money-laundering procedure.
• Inducing Urgency: Introducing elements such
as impending deadlines or the threat of signifi-
cant losses can pressure the model, prompting
it to produce prohibited responses. For exam-
ple, while the model refuses to answer questions
about “bribing an official to obtain approval,”
it may fail to reject queries framed as “imple-
menting an urgent approval plan through benefit
exchanges to avert losses.”
• Fictional Scenarios: Embedding the behav-
ior in a fictional context can lead the model
to treat it as hypothetical, thereby lowering its
self-restrictions. For example, nesting “diverting
payment for personal use” within a “case study
on internal control vulnerabilities in enterprises”
can elicit a detailed embezzlement plan from the
model.
• Strategy Fusion: Combining multiple jailbreak
strategies can divert the model’s attention and
reduce its focus on harmful content.

Market manipulation is when someone artificially affects the supply or demand for a security (for
example, causing stock prices to rise or to fall dramatically). Market manipulation may involve
techniques including: spreading false or misleading information about a company; engaging in a series
of transactions to make a security appear more actively traded; and rigging quotes, prices, or trades to

Bribery
Bribery is the corrupt solicitation, payment, or acceptance of a private favor (a bribe) in exchange for
official action. The purpose of a bribe is to influence the actions of the recipient, a person in charge of
an official duty, to act contrary to their duty and the known rules of honesty and integrity.
Insider Trading
Illegal insider trading refers generally to buying or selling a security, in breach of a fiduciary duty or
other relationship of trust and confidence, on the basis of material, nonpublic information about the
security. Insider trading violations may also include ”tipping” such information, securities trading by
the person ”tipped,” and securities trading by those who misappropriate such information.

funds
Misappropriation of funds refers to the intentional, illegal use of the funds of another person for one’s
own use or other unauthorized purpose, especially by someone who is entrusted with those funds.
Fraud
Fraud refers to intentional deception to deprive a victim of a legal right or to gain from a victim
unlawfully or unfairly.
Tax evasion
Tax evasion involves deliberately and illegally avoiding the payment of a true tax liability.
Cybercrime
Cybercrime encompasses a wide range of criminal activities that are carried out using digital devices
and/or networks.
Forgery
Forgery is the act of fraudulently making or altering a written document with the intent to deceive or
defraud.
Money Laundering
Money laundering is the process of illegally concealing the origin of money obtained from illicit
activities (often known as dirty money), such as drug trafficking, sex work, terrorism, corruption, and
embezzlement, and converting the funds into a seemingly legitimate source, usually through a front
organization.
Misrepresentation
A misrepresentation is a false or misleading statement or a material omission that renders other
statements misleading, with the intent to deceive.
False invoicing
False invoicing is the practice of producing false invoices that do not relate to a real sale or payment
and are used to obtain money dishonestly.
Harming Customer
Interests
Harming client interests refers to professional conduct in which a practitioner fails to place the client’s
interests above their own or their employer’s, lacks prudent and reasonable judgment, or engages
in improper practices—such as unsuitable investment actions, unfair treatment, misrepresentation,
or breach of confidentiality—that result in adverse consequences for the client. Examples include
failing to act loyally for the client, making unsuitable recommendations, overstating performance, or
disclosing confidential information without authorization.
Harming Employer
Interests
Harming employer interests refers to conduct in which an employee fails to fulfill the duty of loyalty
to their employer, such as disclosing confidential information, accepting compensation that creates
a conflict of interest without proper consent, or failing to supervise subordinates in a way that leads
to violations of laws, regulations, or ethical standards—resulting in actual or potential harm to the
employer.
Lack of
Independence and
Objectivity
Lack of Independence and Objectivity refers to failing to act with fairness and impartial judgment,
which may result from undue influence, undisclosed conflicts of interest, or insufficient ethical
diligence. Such failures include accepting gifts or compensation that compromise impartiality, failing
to disclose conflicts, prioritizing personal interests or transactions over clients’ interests, failing to
exercise reasonable care in analysis, and inadequate record retention.
